A strategy contingent on past play, in which a particular past action triggers a different action

stem: Under a grim trigger strategy, what does a firm do after its rival cheats once?
choices: Plays the one-shot Nash (punishment) strategy forever
explain: The threat of permanent punishment is what makes cheating unattractive.

stem: In i* = (π_c − π_n) / (π_d − π_c), what does the denominator measure?
explain: Cheat payoff minus collusive payoff, earned once.

stem: Collusion with trigger strategies is sustainable when the interest rate is:
choices: At or below the threshold i*
explain: Low interest rates make the future punishment matter.

stem: True or false: For a trigger strategy to work, cheating must be detected so the rival knows to punish.
explain: True. Undetected cheating cannot trigger punishment.

stem: A firm can raise the payoff it gets in the punishment phase (for example, by having a cheaper backup product). What does that do to collusion?
choices: Makes collusion harder: punishment hurts less, so i* falls
explain: π_n rises, so (π_c − π_n) falls and so does i*.

stem: A price-matching guarantee punishes a rival's price cut automatically. How does this relate to trigger strategies?
choices: It makes punishment fast and certain, supporting collusion

stem: Why must a trigger-strategy punishment be the one-shot Nash outcome (or something else each firm would actually carry out)?
choices: Otherwise the threat to punish is not credible
explain: The one-shot Nash outcome has each firm best-responding, so it will really happen.
